newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac faces delicate task on franc, policies.
newsitem.headline: Chirac faces delicate task on franc, policies.

text.p: Financial markets will closely watch President Jacques Chirac's television interview on Thursday for signs of deviation from his support for the Bank of France's commitment to a stable franc, but few expect to see them.

Because any such deviation would provoke a pummelling of the franc by international investors, Chirac is left with the delicate task of lifting his electorate's morale while forcing it to accept that there will be no change in the tough economic policies aimed at qualifying France for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
The result is likely to be a series of guarded statements on prickly issues which will be as unresolved after the television appearance as they are now, analysts said.

"The great difficulty for Chirac will be to hold the course on the big orientations for Europe while lifting the morale of the French," Banques Populaires economist Herve Goulletquer said. "He is a little bit stuck."
These issues include taxes, employment, monetary union and the franc/mark parity, economists said.
The franc/mark parity is among the most important and sensitive of them but also the one on which Chirac has the least room to manoeuvre.

"I just can't see him reversing himself on an issue that has been the work of all of France for over 10 years," Goulletquer said about talk that France might soften its commitment to the so called franc fort policy.

Markets have been on tenterhooks since a resurgence in mid-November of a debate on France's decade-long commitment to keeping the franc pegged to the mark, even when this has meant raising domestic interest rates, slowing economic growth and hurting French competitiveness.

Chirac has been known in the past to make remarks which have unnerved financial markets -- for example in July, his last major television appearance, he said he believed interest rates in France and Germany were too high.
His comments, suggesting he was at odds with the Bank of France over its cautious monetary policy, started a long fuse which led in August to a mini-franc crisis.

Market analysts will be waiting for the president to reaffirm once again his commitment to embattled Prime Minister Alain Juppe and the tough economic policies aimed at qualifying France for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

"I would be very surprised to hear him say anything that deviates from his support of EMU," Merrill Lynch economist Darren Williams said. "He's going to give some indication of his support for Juppe."
The debate on the franc was relaunched by former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing last month when he called for a sharp depreciation of the franc to revive economic growth.
His call was joined by leading politicians and even some members of the Bank of France monetary policy council.
It was firmly opposed by Juppe, members of the government and Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet.

Giscard's comments never got a hint of support from Chirac, but given the Gaullist president's overt concern over poor economic growth, many in the market suspect they might have struck a chord with the president.
